title: Ezekiel 22:1–16
context: Ezekiel reports the LORD’s word charging him, as “son of man,” to judge “the bloody city,” Jerusalem, and make known her abominations (22:1–2). The LORD indicts the city for bloodshed and idolatry (22:3–5) and lists the sins of its princes and people: contempt for parents, oppression of the foreigner, fatherless, and widow, profaned Sabbaths, slander, idolatrous meals, sexual wrongs within families, bribery, interest, and extortion, all summed up as having “forgotten me” (22:6–12). He will scatter the city among the nations and purge its filthiness (22:13–16).

verses.text: Moreover the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel reports, “Moreover the LORD’s word came to me.” Arminian readers see the prophet receiving a word he did not invent, which sets his message apart from the false prophets named later in 22:28.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the authority of the oracle in its divine source. Readers in this tradition note that Ezekiel regularly introduces his messages this way, stressing that the indictment that follows is the LORD’s own.

verses.text: “You, son of man, will you judge? Will you judge the bloody city? Then cause her to know all her abominations.
verses.arminianNotes: “You, son of man, will you judge? Will you judge the bloody city?” Arminian readers hear the LORD commissioning Ezekiel to confront Jerusalem with its sins so that it might know them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a summons to prosecute the case against Jerusalem. The address “son of man” stresses Ezekiel’s humanity before God, and readers in this tradition see the call as a charge to declare the city’s guilt.

verses.text: You shall say, ‘The Lord GOD says: “A city that sheds blood within herself, that her time may come, and that makes idols against herself to defile her!
verses.arminianNotes: “A city that sheds blood within herself, that her time may come, and that makes idols against herself to defile her!” Arminian readers see violence and idolatry bringing judgment on the city by its own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see bloodshed and idolatry as the twin charges against Jerusalem. Readers in this tradition note the phrase “against herself,” showing that the city’s sins harm the city itself.

verses.text: You have become guilty in your blood that you have shed, and are defiled in your idols which you have made! You have caused your days to draw near, and have come to the end of your years. Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations, and a mocking to all the countries.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have become guilty in your blood that you have shed, and are defiled in your idols which you have made!” Arminian readers see Jerusalem hastening its own end through its sins.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see guilt and defilement joined. “You have caused your days to draw near” presents judgment as the fruit of the city’s conduct, and readers in this tradition see the LORD’s justice in it.

verses.text: Those who are near and those who are far from you will mock you, you infamous one, full of tumult.
verses.arminianNotes: “Those who are near and those who are far from you will mock you, you infamous one, full of tumult.” Arminian readers see Jerusalem’s disgrace before the nations as a consequence of its sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the city’s reputation ruined. Readers in this tradition note the contrast with the honor God intended for Jerusalem among the nations, now turned to mockery.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Behold, the princes of Israel, everyone according to his power, have been in you to shed blood.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, the princes of Israel, everyone according to his power, have been in you to shed blood.” Arminian readers see leaders abusing their power, each according to the strength they held.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see rulers held responsible for violence. Readers in this tradition note that the list of sins begins with the princes, showing that those with the most power bear heavy accountability.

verses.text: In you have they treated father and mother with contempt. Among you they have oppressed the foreigner. In you they have wronged the fatherless and the widow.
verses.arminianNotes: “In you have they treated father and mother with contempt.” Arminian readers see the breakdown of family honor and the oppression of the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see violations of the commandments to honor parents and protect the vulnerable. Readers in this tradition note that care for the foreigner, fatherless, and widow is a frequent test of covenant faithfulness.

verses.text: You have despised my holy things, and have profaned my Sabbaths.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have despised my holy things, and have profaned my Sabbaths.” Arminian readers see contempt for worship joined with injustice, since both reflect a turning away from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see sins against God’s holy things and Sabbaths alongside sins against neighbors. Readers in this tradition note that Ezekiel 20:12 calls the Sabbaths a sign between God and his people.

verses.text: Slanderous men have been in you to shed blood. In you they have eaten on the mountains. They have committed lewdness among you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Slanderous men have been in you to shed blood. In you they have eaten on the mountains.” Arminian readers see slander leading to violence, and idolatrous meals at the high places named among the sins.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a list of sins that join false witness, idolatry, and immorality. Eating on the mountains appears among the sins in 18:6, and readers in this tradition take it as idolatrous worship.

verses.text: In you have they uncovered their fathers’ nakedness. In you have they humbled her who was unclean in her impurity.
verses.arminianNotes: The verse names sexual sins within families and against a woman in her impurity. Arminian readers read the charges soberly as violations of the laws of Leviticus 18, cited by reference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the charges with restraint, as breaches of the holiness laws of Leviticus 18 and 20, cited by reference. Readers in this tradition note that these sins harm the vulnerable and defile the community.

verses.text: One has committed abomination with his neighbor’s wife, and another has lewdly defiled his daughter-in-law. Another in you has humbled his sister, his father’s daughter.
verses.arminianNotes: The verse continues the list of sexual wrongs within neighbors’ and family relationships. Arminian readers see the corruption of trust in the closest relationships, read soberly and without detail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see grave violations of family and covenant boundaries. Readers in this tradition treat the verse as part of the indictment, noting how widely sin had spread through the city’s households.

verses.text: In you have they taken bribes to shed blood. You have taken interest and increase, and you have greedily gained of your neighbors by oppression, and have forgotten me,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: “In you have they taken bribes to shed blood. You have taken interest and increase … and have forgotten me,” says the Lord GOD. Arminian readers see economic oppression rooted in forgetting God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see bribery, usury, and extortion summed up as forgetting the LORD. Readers in this tradition note that injustice toward neighbors is treated as a failure toward God himself.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Behold, therefore I have struck my hand at your dishonest gain which you have made, and at the blood which has been shed within you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, therefore I have struck my hand at your dishonest gain which you have made, and at the blood which has been shed within you.” Arminian readers see God’s indignant gesture against injustice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s judgment against greed and bloodshed. Readers in this tradition note that striking the hand is a gesture of displeasure found elsewhere in Ezekiel, as in 21:17.

verses.text: Can your heart endure, or can your hands be strong, in the days that I will deal with you? I, the LORD, have spoken it, and will do it.
verses.arminianNotes: “Can your heart endure, or can your hands be strong, in the days that I will deal with you? I, the LORD, have spoken it, and will do it.” Arminian readers see human strength failing before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the certainty of God’s word of judgment. Readers in this tradition stress that what the LORD speaks he will do, a truth that warns the city and comforts the faithful.

verses.text: I will scatter you among the nations, and disperse you through the countries. I will purge your filthiness out of you.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will scatter you among the nations, and disperse you through the countries. I will purge your filthiness out of you.” Arminian readers see exile as judgment with a purifying purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see scattering as both punishment and purging. Readers in this tradition note that the LORD aims to remove the city’s filthiness, showing that judgment serves his holy purposes.

verses.text: You will be profaned in yourself in the sight of the nations. Then you will know that I am the LORD.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “You will be profaned in yourself in the sight of the nations. Then you will know that I am the LORD.” Arminian readers see judgment leading to knowledge of God, a recurring aim in Ezekiel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the familiar refrain “you will know that I am the LORD.” Readers in this tradition see God revealing himself through judgment as well as through mercy.
